counterexample: Take the point A = (1, 0), which lies on the x-axis Ox (equation y = 0). By the definition of L in step 0002, L(x, y) = (x, x + y), so L(A) = (1, 1 + 0) = (1, 1). Step 0009 asserts that the image L(Ox) is the line with equation x + y = 0. But L(A) = (1, 1) gives x + y = 1 + 1 = 2 != 0, so the image point L(A) does NOT lie on the asserted line. Conversely, the point P = (-1, 1) satisfies x + y = 0, yet its unique L-preimage is (x, y) with x = -1 and x + y = 1, i.e. y = 2, so the preimage is (-1, 2), which does not lie on Ox (y = 2 != 0); hence P is not in L(Ox) either. So the asserted line neither contains nor is contained in L(Ox). The true image is L(Ox) = { (x, x) : x in R }, the line y = x (equation x - y = 0), since (x, 0) maps to (x, x). The set x + y = 0 is in fact the PREIMAGE L^{-1}(Ox) (from (x, y) |-> (x, x + y) landing on y = 0, i.e. x + y = 0), so step 0009 substituted forward instead of using the inverse map and reported the preimage as the image. Numerical check of both directions: L(2, 0) = (2, 2), on y = x, off x + y = 0; L(-2, 2) = (-2, 0) — this point is on Ox, and its source (-2, 2) is on the claimed line x + y = 0, confirming that x + y = 0 is the preimage, not the image.
reasoning_summary: Steps 0001-0002 set up a counterexample strategy with L(x, y) = (x, x + y), which is well defined. Steps 0004-0007 are correct: L(A) - L(B) = (x_A - x_B, (x_A + y_A) - (x_B + y_B)) = (x_AB, x_AB + y_AB), a linear function of the vector AB, so L is affine (in fact linear). Step 0009 is where verification fails. The image of Ox (y = 0) under L is { (x, x) } = the line y = x, i.e. x - y = 0, not x + y = 0 as claimed; the set x + y = 0 is the preimage of Ox, obtained by the common error of substituting the forward map into the equation rather than the inverse. (The claim about Oy in the same step is correct: (0, y) maps to (0, y), so L(Oy) is x = 0.) I stopped at step 0009 with the explicit witness A = (1, 0) |-> (1, 1). Note in fairness that the theorem itself is true and the numerical value pi/4 quoted in step 0011 happens to be right anyway, since the correct image line y = x also makes an angle of pi/4 with the y-axis; but as written the proof's step 0009 states a false identification of the transformed line, so the chain of justification as given does not hold at that step.
